The first area that we looked at was grade book type. The updated policy 2418 requires us to use a consistent grade book type across our schools. You can see here that the recommendation from the committee was to move to the rolling gradebook, but not until school year 26-27.

The committee recommended that we use school year 25-26 to make sure that everybody is trained sufficiently and has the support and resources and time that they need to make the shift to the rolling gradebook. And I think that's a really wise recommendation because we know previously when sometimes we've seen some of our school communities make more sudden changes to grading practice practices has been quite disruptive to the community and caused confusion for some students, parents, and staff.

So in terms of the rationale for this particular recommendation, the folks that looked at the current use of rolling grade book in terms of who's currently using it and pointing out benefits from that group, the rolling grade book really does allow for more flexibility both in reassessment practices as well as course design.

So rolling grade book again differs from traditional grade book in that the grade book is open from the first day of school until the last day of school. A traditional quarterly grade book closes each quarter and then a student's grade is average from quarter to quarter over the course of the semester or over the course of the full year.

And most of our secondary courses are full year courses. But with a rolling grade book, students can go back and demonstrate mastery on a particular learning standard or skill that maybe they started in the first quarter, but they didn't quite master it yet but by the third quarter they've mastered it and they can get credit for that continuation of working towards mastery so it provides more flexibility more support for student learning additionally when the committee looked at this you can see that most of our schools are using the rolling gradebook 66% of our high schools use the rolling gradebook exclusively as of today and when we include middle schools in that 63% of

our middle schools and high schools use the rolling grade book in at least some capacity. That means there might be a school where some teachers use rolling grade book in that school and others use the quarterly grade book. So again, because of the flexibility and because of the high use of current use of the rolling grade book, the committee is recommending implementation for 26-27.

Next area that we looked at was grade weighting. So 24-18, policy 24-18 does require consistent weighting with a balanced and fair approach between formative and summative categories. So again, for folks in the community, when we're talking about summative tasks, we're talking about those assignments, those tasks that might be at the end of a learning unit, at the end of a quarter, at the end of a school year, for example, as opposed to formative tasks where students have the opportunity to continue to practice their learning and to get feedback from their teachers.

So the summatives are kind of the culminating activity, and the formatives are process-oriented and practice-oriented. So the committee here recommended maintaining the current district gradebook weighting of 70% summative and 30% formative.

And again, you can see the committee percentages at the bottom of each of these slides. So this was 93% concurrence on this. And in terms of the rationale, we have seen that the consistency of parents and students reporting that they understand their students' grades has increased significantly.

In fact, when we surveyed the different groups, only 9% of our students, 12% of parents, and 19% of staff reported that our current weighting of 70 summative, 30 formative is not working well for them. Again, the vast majority are reporting that 70, 30 is working well for them right now.

We did look on this particular recommendation to see if there was any interest with our department chairs and administrators in differentiating the category weighting by content area. So for example, maybe you have 70/30 in the core content areas.

Maybe you have 80/20 in the elective areas or the fine arts or CTE areas. However, in discussion with our department chairs and administrators, we were not able to reach any consensus on what a standardization might look like in different content areas. There was a lot of disagreement about what that might look like and given the fact that the policy calls for fair and balanced and consistent weighting, the committee ultimately recommended that all teachers use the 70-30 weighting.

Okay, so the next recommendation was around homework, and policy 24-18 was updated of course to really promote the importance of consistent use of homework as regular opportunities for student practice, and the committee looked at this and did recommend maintaining our current homework practices, which currently allow teachers to use the formative category that 30 percent of a student's weight to provide homework grades.

The considerations really around this was looking at the data about current use around homework. You can see at the supporting evidence there that when we look at our use survey results, almost 92 percent of our secondary students report having daily homework, and you can see the amount ranges all the way up to daily homework of over half of our students at the eighth grade saying they spend more than an hour a day on homework to two-thirds of our students at the twelfth grade saying they spend more than an hour a day on homework.

When we process this through with our staff and focus groups and at the committee there was a lot of disagreement about creating a separate category for waiting homework. I think the main reason or one of the main reasons for that was the concern about having to grade homework and the workload that would be associated with that.

So, again, committee recommended maintaining our current practices. Now, I want to point out, though, that the committee, again, has been fantastic in terms of their dedication to this work. But some members of senior leadership, of course, have had other conversations with community members outside of the committee process and have had conversations really through the entire process of the board's development of policy 2418.

And when we looked at the homework recommendation from the committee, our senior leadership team felt that we really needed to establish a set category for homework weighting. And that we thought that the best way to do that would be to establish homework weighting category at 10% of a student's grade.

And the reason for that is while students are reporting consistent homework right now, we're not at 100% of those experiences. And I shared that data just a minute ago, how it varies kind of from 50% to two-thirds over grade eight through grade 12 that have consistently reporting homework.

So with the belief around our increased focus on academic rigor in all the areas of our strategic plan, the research around consistent homework and practice supporting student learning, our senior leadership team felt strongly that we should weight it at 10% of a student's grade.

If we do that, and if the board accepts that alternative recommendation, that obviously is going to impact the category weighting. Because currently homework is part of that 30% formative grade. So if we take homework, make it a separate 10%, that's going to impact our summative percentage and our formative percentage.

So the second alternative recommendation that you see here would be to change the category weighting to 60% summative, 30% formative, and 10% homework. And when we look at the board's guidance in policy 2418 that creates an expectation for a fair and balanced approach between the formative and summative categories, 60-40 basically is getting us, I think, better balance than 70-30.

So that's how our senior leadership team developed that recommendation as an alternative to the committee. Okay, the next area is around reassessment. So policy 2418 also requires consistent reassessment practices that would provide students one opportunity to reassess for each summative assessment that they take and you can see that the committee's recommendation here is to maintain the current practice which allows students to earn up to a hundred percent credit on those reassessments that they complete now just as a reminder before a student completes a reassessment we do have requirements that they take action

to ensure that they have done additional work before a teacher provides them with a reassessment opportunity, so that might look like test corrections, additional homework assignments that need to be completed to prepare for that reassessment.

So when we look at the feedback on this particular recommendation, though, again, what you'll notice is that there was obviously a difference of opinion on this particular recommendation across the different groups in our school system. So for example, our students and family members were very clear that the change to 100% this year was a very positive change that lowered stress levels for them, increased their motivation both on the original assessments and on reassessments. So we see that very clearly in the survey data as well as the focus groups that we ran. However, I also want to be very clear that

we heard loudly and strongly from our teachers that they did not view the change to 100% reassessment positively, and largely that was due to increased workload. So 51% of our teachers said that they had a significant increase in workload with reassessment to 100 percent.

Ultimately, well, I should point out there is the bullet point about the study that I mentioned earlier around reassessment, and this is a relatively new study. So this particular study looked at math performance at the secondary level and studied the impact of a reassessment policy allowing up to 100 percent and found that student learning growth was increased between 36% to 45% when students were allowed to reassess to 100% in those math classes.

So ultimately, taking all of this into consideration, the committee felt like our current practice was manageable, recognizing the teacher workload issues. They felt it was manageable if we provided very clear guidance and support to our teachers about practices for reassessment that could address workload, and I want to share a few of those ideas with you next.

So really to that end around reducing teacher workload, the committee recommended professional learning on specific practices to alleviate those concerns like the ones that you see here. So, for example, focusing reassessments on the specific standards or skills that students had not mastered.

So instead of, let's just pretend you gave a 50 question test, instead of reassessing another 50 questions, maybe students only were struggling with 10 of the questions. You could create a smaller reassessment of 10 questions on those topics that students hadn't mastered, saving time in the grading process.

Obviously, there's still workload associated with reassessment, but that starts to mitigate that somewhat. Additionally, when we hear from teachers that sometimes students want to reassess where they had like a 95 and they want to get that 100, well, there might only be one or two questions that a student would need to retake, and you might actually be able to do that in a conversation with the student, or you might be able to do that in a simple test correction.

Maybe a student made a calculation error on a math exam, but giving that student an opportunity to redo that one item certainly would be a lot less work than asking them to retest on every one of the concepts from the original test and have to grade that again.

We know that it's difficult to find time to do the reassessment, but when we use that learning seminar time built into the schedule and when we work to really try to utilize time in class for reassessments, that can reduce some of the workload issues as well. So the committee felt very strongly, again, that if we continue with the 100 percent reassessment policy, we certainly want to make resources and training available to staff on some strategies to address workload concerns.
